According to the plaintiff, these persons were the original bhoomidars of the suit land.
The suit property is described as forming part of Khasra No. 7/2. 21.3
These documents, however, are unreliable for four reasons.
First, the khatoni Ex. PW6/A reflects that none of the aforesaid persons were bhoomidars of land comprised in Khasra No. 7/2.
The principle nemo dat quod non habet - no one can transfer a better title than he himself possesses -
squarely applies.

Since Bhagwan,
Raghubir, Zile, and Suresh were not owners of the suit property, they could not have conveyed it to Ram Adhar.

21.4 PW4, the husband of Pinki, was examined by the plaintiff and he deposed that he did not verify the ownership of the suit property or check the land records before it was purchased by him in the name of his wife.
Contrary to the case of the plaintiff, he deposed that defendant no.1 and 2 had sought permission from him to reside in one room on the ground that RICHA GUSAIN they were expecting a child.
SOLANKI CS DJ ADJ No. 517710/2016 Shivji Parit vs Ramwati & Ors Page no. 7/12 21.5 Second, a GPA, affidavit, and receipt do not, in law, constitute a valid mode of transfer of immovable property.

Reference may be made to Section 54 of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882, and Sections 17 and 49 of the Registration Act, 1908, which provide as follows:
"Section 54.
"Sale" defined.-- "Sale" is a transfer of ownership in exchange for a price paid or promised or part-paid and part- promised.

Sale how made.--Such transfer, in the case of tangible immovable property of the value of one hundred rupees and upwards, or in the case of a reversion or other intangible thing, can be made only by a registered instrument.
In the case of tangible immovable property of a value less than one hundred rupees, such transfer may be made either by a registered instrument or by delivery of the property.
Delivery of tangible immovable property takes place when the seller places the buyer, or such person as he directs, in possession of the property.
Contract for
sale.--A contract for the sale of immovable property is a contract that a sale of such property shall take place on terms settled between the parties.
It does not, of itself, create any interest in or charge on such property."

"Section 17. Documents of which registration is compulsory.--

The chain of documents marked Ex. PW9/C does not effect any transfer of title in respect of the suit property.
Consequently, the very foundation of the plaintiff's claim stands vitiated.
21.7 Third, all three sets of documents contain overwriting.
The notation "Khasra No. 7/2" appears to have been written over "Khasra No. 7/5", which has not been explained by the plaintiff or his witnesses.

The plaintiff merely states that the correction was done by the deed writer in hand, but does not clarify whether the same was done before signing of the documents, and such correction was approved by the parties executing it.
21.8 Fourth, the plaintiff did not summon any of the executants or attesting witnesses to prove the execution of the documents comprising Ex. PW9/C or to explain the overwriting therein.

21.9 The next set of documents, Ex. PW9/B - comprising a GPA,
ATS, affidavit, receipt, Will and possession letter dated 09.01.2012 executed by Ram Adhar in favour of Pinki - also fail RICHA to sustain the plaintiff's case.

Moreover,
they suffer from the same legal infirmity: they do not constitute a valid transfer of immovable property within the meaning of Section 54 of the Transfer of Property Act, and the executant was not produced to prove their execution.

Notably, these six documents also contain identical overwriting - "Khasra No. 7/5"
corrected to "Khasra No. 7/2".
21.10

Similarly, the documents forming Ex. PW9/A - namely the GPA, ATS, affidavit, receipt, Will and possession letter dated 25.06.2012 executed by Pinki in favour of the plaintiff - suffer from the same defects.
They purport to effect transfer of immovable property through unregistered documents and contain the same overwriting: "Khasra No. 7/5" altered to "Khasra No. 7/2".

21.11 While a correction in a typed document may be explained as an inadvertent error in a single transaction, it is highly implausible that the same error would recur in another set of six documents executed twenty-five years later, and yet again in another set executed six months thereafter.

This casts a serious doubt on the identity of the property described in documents Ex. PW9/A to Ex.
PW9/C. 21.12
Further, the plaintiff's own witness- PW3 admitted that the suit property did not fall in khasra no. 7/2 but 5/2.
He also admitted that it did not ad-measure of 68 yd., as claimed by the plaintiff but 65 yd.
as claimed by defendant nos. 1 to 3. 21.13

Accordingly, the plaintiff has failed to establish the genuineness of the documents dated 25.06.2012 and, therefore, RICHA cannot be held to have acquired any right, title or interest in the GUSAIN suit property on the basis thereof.

The chain of documents marked Ex. PW9/C does not effect any transfer of title in respect of the suit property.
Moreover,
they suffer from the same legal infirmity: they do not constitute a valid transfer of immovable property within the meaning of Section 54 of the Transfer of Property Act, and the executant was not produced to prove their execution.
Notably, these six documents also contain identical overwriting - "Khasra No. 7/5"
corrected to "Khasra No. 7/2".
21.10
They purport to effect transfer of immovable property through unregistered documents and contain the same overwriting: "Khasra No. 7/5" altered to "Khasra No. 7/2".
Accordingly, the plaintiff has failed to establish the genuineness of the documents dated 25.06.2012 and, therefore, RICHA cannot be held to have acquired any right, title or interest in the GUSAIN suit property on the basis thereof.
